{{short description|Claimed as largest named number}}
'''Rayo's number''' is a [[large number]] named after Mexican philosophy professor [[Agustín Rayo]], who defined it during a "Big Number Duel" at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) on 26 January 2007.<ref>{{cite web |last=Elga |first=Adam |title=Large Number Championship |url=http://web.mit.edu/philosophy/poster.pdf |accessdate=24 March 2014 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20190714053228/http://web.mit.edu/philosophy/poster.pdf |archivedate=14 July 2019 }}</ref><ref name="tech">{{cite news |last=Manzari |first=Mandana |title=Profs Duke It Out in Big Number Duel |url=http://tech.mit.edu/V126/N64/64largenumber.html |accessdate=24 March 2014 |newspaper=The Tech |date=31 January 2007 |author2=Nick Semenkovich |archive-date=19 September 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080919124735/http://tech.mit.edu/V126/N64/64largenumber.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> At the time, it was claimed to be the largest named number, as its size vastly exceeds even other notable large numbers such as [[Graham's number]] and [[Kruskal's tree theorem|TREE(3)]].<ref>{{cite web| title=CH. Rayo's Number |url=http://mathfactor.uark.edu/2007/04/ch-rayos-number/ |publisher=The Math Factor Podcast |accessdate=24 March 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Kerr |first=Josh |title=Name the biggest number contest |url=http://joshkerr.com/who-can-name-the-bigger-number-contest/ |accessdate=27 March 2014 |date=7 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320033110/http://www.joshkerr.com/who-can-name-the-bigger-number-contest/ |archive-date=20 March 2016 }}</ref> 

== Definition ==
The definition of Rayo's number is a variation on the definition:<ref name="rayo">{{cite web |last=Rayo |first=Agustín |title=Big Number Duel |url=http://web.mit.edu/arayo/www/bignums.html |accessdate=24 March 2014}}</ref>

<blockquote>The smallest number bigger than any finite number named by an expression in any language of [[set theory|first-order set theory]] in which the language uses only a [[googol]] symbols or less.</blockquote>

Specifically, an initial version of the definition, which was later clarified, read "The smallest number bigger than any number that can be named by an expression in the language of first-order set-theory with less than a googol ({{10^|100}}) symbols".<ref name="tech" />

The formal definition of the number defines a predicate <math>\mbox{Sat}</math> according to the following [[Second-order logic|second-order]] formula, where <math>[\phi]</math> is a [[Gödel numbering|Gödel-coded]] formula and <math>s</math> is a variable assignment:<ref name="rayo" />
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mbox{Sat}([\phi],s):=    & \mbox{For all }R \ \{ \\
    & \{ \mbox{for any (coded) formula } [\psi] \mbox{ and any variable assignment } t \\
    & (R([\psi],t) \leftrightarrow \\
    & (( [\psi] = \mbox{''}x_i \in x_j\mbox{''} \and t(x_i) \in t(x_j)) \ \or \\
    & ( [\psi] = \mbox{''}x_i = x_j\mbox{''} \and t(x_i) = t(x_j)) \ \or \\
    & ( [\psi] = \mbox{''}(\neg \theta)\mbox{''} \and \neg R([\theta],t)) \ \or \\
    & ( [\psi] = \mbox{''}(\theta \and \xi)\mbox{''} \and R([\theta],t) \and R([\xi],t)) \ \or \\
    & ( [\psi] = \mbox{''}\exists x_i \ (\theta)\mbox{'' and, for some an } x_i \mbox{-variant } t' \mbox{ of } t, R([\theta],t')) \\
    & )\} \rightarrow \\
    & R([\phi],s)\}
\end{align}</math>

Given this formula, Rayo's number is defined as:<ref name="rayo" />

<blockquote>The smallest number bigger than every finite number <math>m</math> with the following property: there is a formula <math>\phi(x_1)</math> in the language of first-order set-theory (as presented in the definition of <math>\mbox{Sat}</math>) with less than a googol symbols and <math>x_1</math> as its only free variable such that: (a) there is a variable assignment <math>s</math> assigning <math>m</math> to <math>x_1</math> such that <math>\mbox{Sat}([\phi(x_1)],s)</math>, and (b) for any variable assignment <math>t</math>, if <math>\mbox{Sat}([\phi(x_1)],t)</math>, then <math>t</math> assigns <math>m</math> to <math>x_1</math>.</blockquote>

== Explanation ==
Intuitively, Rayo's number is defined in a [[formal language]], such that:
* <math>x_i \in x_j</math> and <math>x_i = x_j</math> are [[atomic formulas]].
* If <math>\theta</math> is a formula, then <math>(\neg\theta)</math> is a formula (the [[negation]] of <math>\theta</math>).
* If <math>\theta</math> and <math>\xi</math> are formulas, then <math>(\theta \and \xi)</math> is a formula (the [[logical conjunction|conjunction]] of <math>\theta</math> and <math>\xi</math>).
* If <math>\theta</math> is a formula, then <math>\exists x_i(\theta)</math> is a formula ([[existential quantification]]).

It is not allowed to eliminate parentheses. For instance, one must write <math>\exists x_i((\neg \theta))</math> instead of <math>\exists x_i(\neg \theta)</math>.

It is possible to express the missing [[logical connectives]] in this language. For instance:
* [[logical disjunction|Disjunction]]: <math>(\theta \or \xi)</math> as <math>(\neg((\neg \theta)\and(\neg \xi)))</math>.
* [[material conditional|Implication]]: <math>(\theta \Rightarrow \xi)</math> as <math>(\neg(\theta \and(\neg \xi)))</math>.
* [[Biconditional]]: <math>(\theta \Leftrightarrow \xi)</math> as <math>(\neg((\neg(\theta \and \xi))\and(\neg((\neg \theta) \and (\neg \xi)))))</math>.
* [[Universal quantification]]: <math>\forall x_i(\theta)</math> as <math>(\neg \exists x_i((\neg \theta)))</math>.

The definition concerns formulas in this language that have only one [[free variable]], specifically <math>x_1</math>. If a formula with length <math>n</math> is satisfied [[iff]] <math>x_1</math> is equal to the finite [[von Neumann ordinal]] <math>k</math>, we say such a formula is a "Rayo string" for <math>k</math>, and that <math>k</math> is "Rayo-nameable" in <math>n</math> symbols. Then, <math>\mbox{Rayo}(10^{100})</math> is defined as the smallest <math>k</math> greater than all numbers Rayo-nameable in at most <math>(10^{100})</math> symbols.

Rayo notes that mathematicians working with a nonrealist philosophy of math may reject Rayo's number as being well-defined, because any [[Computably enumerable set|computably enumerable]] axiomatization of the language of second-order logic will have non-isomorphic [[Structure (mathematical logic)|models]], under which Rayo's number could correspond to different values.<ref name="rayo" />
